Analysis by Richard Cowan 

MarijuanaNews.com generally focuses as much on media criticism as reporting, so I generally like to wait to see how an event will be reported. Last week’s report on the Schafer/Fry case was an exception, because I thought that both the case and the context were important. 

See 

In Occupied California Schafer/Fry Case Federal Judge More Sympathetic Than Local Narks. Insane War on Medical Cannabis And Echoes of New Orleans.

Ironically, I managed to miss a very important development that happened the day after the Sacramento County supervisors cited federal law as an excuse refuse to issue county medical marijuana ID cards to patients.

 

As usual, they were listening to local law enforcement, not the people who elected them. Both Sacramento County Sheriff John McGinness and District Attorney Jan Scully had argued against the program. The Sheriff claimed, "We have a conflict. We are talking about a behavior that is illegal by federal law." 

However, the very next day, there in Sacramento, the State Supreme Court refused to hear an appeal of Garden Grove v. Superior Court , in which the Superior Court (an appeals court) had ruled last November that a medical marijuana patient, Felix Kha, was entitled to get his cannabis back from law enforcement.

 

Moreover, the California Supreme Court ruled that the Superior Court’s opinion would remain “published” – meaning that it is binding on all other California Superior Courts and officials, and that California officials are bound by the State Constitution to obey and enforce state – not federal – laws. 

Since the victory of Prop 215 in 1996, California law enforcement has claimed that they could not comply with the state’s medical cannabis laws because they conflicted with federal law, even though the state constitution explicitly says in Article III, Section 3.5 (adopted in 1978) that "An administrative agency, including an administrative agency created by the Constitution or an initiative statute, has no power: ... (c) to declare a statute unenforceable, or to refuse to enforce a statute, on the basis that federal law or federal regulations prohibit the enforcement of such statute unless an appellate court has made a determination that the enforcement of such a statute is prohibited by federal law or federal regulations." 

From 1999, see 

California Constitution Specifically Prohibits State Officials From Using Federal Laws As An Excuse For Not Enforcing State Laws Like Prop 215 Without A Court Ruling. Great Orange County Register Editorial.

The most direct conflict between state and federal laws occurred – as in the Kha case – when the police refused to obey state court orders to return medical cannabis to a patient that they had seized in an arrest in which the charges had been dropped, falsely claiming that they would be in violation of federal law. 

However, federal law provides a loophole, albeit one that was intended to harm rather than help the citizens. 21 U.S.C. Section 885(d) says “no civil or criminal liability shall be imposed [under the federal Controlled Substances Act] upon any... duly authorized officer of any State... who shall be lawfully engaged in the enforcement of any law or municipal ordinance relating to controlled substances.” 

Other times, local law enforcement just chose to ignore the state law and then claim that the federal law was supreme. That was just an excuse for an abuse of power. Steve Kubby was perhaps the most famous victim of law enforcement’s refusal to obey the state law.

See 

Selective Enforcement Versus Selective Compliance – 2 Articles 

and links, especially 

What Part Of 'Exempt' Do California District Attorneys Still Not Understand? Many cities and towns in California have cited federal law in refusing to allow dispensaries to operate in their communities. This ploy will no longer work. 

The Feds were not above taking advantage of the situation either. LA based US Attorney Thomas P. O'Brien won his position by currying favor in the Bush Administration by threatening elected officials in Riverside County with federal prosecution under federal conspiracy laws if they obeyed state rather than federal laws by issuing business licenses to dispensaries. In Cathedral City, California – adjacent to Palm Springs, the city council even tried to get a federal restraining order to close a dispensary. They violated their obligation to uphold the California constitution. 

See 

US Attorney for Northern California Makes Nice, Maybe; LA Counterpart Talks Tough. Berkeley Better Than Oakland? One Nation Under A Bush? 

I would also assume that this ruling will force San Diego and San Bernadino Counties to drop their lawsuits to overturn Prop 215, because it conflicts with federal laws. 

For all the above reasons, it would seem clear that this decision was very important, but the reason that I missed it last week when I was writing about the Sacramento Supervisors and the Schafer/Fry case was that it had not been reported anywhere that I – or even the Mapinc.org newshounds – could find. There is still nothing a week later. 

What makes this blackout even more puzzling is that the LA Times actually editorialized in favor of the Superior Court ruling; however, they did so in an editorial with the incredibly stupid title Wacky Tabacky Case 

For years, I have complained about the media practice of inappropriate humor to condition the reader not to take anything about cannabis seriously.

See 

Canadian Supreme Court Hearings Could Make History, But They Are Only Good For A Joke In DEAland Media. Filed Under Oddly Enough. Dude, Is This Journalism? 

Consider this excerpt from their December 4, 2007 Wacky Tabacky Case editorial and see if you can find anything humorous about it: 

“In 2005, Garden Grove police officers stopped Felix Kha for failing to yield at a red light. Kha consented to a search of his car, and police found one-third of an ounce of marijuana that Kha explained was for medicinal purposes. Orange County prosecutors dismissed drug charges against him after contacting his doctor, and Kha sought the return of his property. The police refused, saying that returning the drug would violate federal laws against marijuana distribution and possession. The Superior Court of Orange County found for Kha, saying the state never convicted him of possessing marijuana illegally and therefore, under California law, the stash was not contraband. Garden Grove appealed.

 

Can a city invoke federal law to justify its recalcitrance in complying with state law? This is where things could have gotten sticky. But the court correctly found that in this case federal law did not take precedence over California law. The federal government is perfectly free to seize Kha's marijuana if it chooses, the court found, but medical marijuana is legal in this state and neither the police nor the courts are charged with enforcing federal law. "We would be astonished if prosecutors began filing federal charges in state courts," the court wrote. 

Numerous law enforcement agencies sided with Garden Grove in its appeal, arguing that returning the marijuana to Kha was practically anti-American. It would turn cops into criminals and damage the high moral standing of local law enforcement, which often cooperates with federal law enforcement. The court responded that police were not likely to be prosecuted for distributing marijuana unless they intentionally began dealing drugs, and that while it's fine for the police to work with federal agencies, their more traditional duty is to uphold state law.” 

Wacky, indeed!
